standard.title: Types of Businesses
standard.description: the reasons businesses exist and how different types of businesses provide goods and services
standard.prior_knowledge: Students have explored consumer choices and how individuals make financial decisions (AC9HS6K08). They are familiar with the idea of goods and services from everyday life but have not formally analysed why businesses exist, the range of business structures, or the distinction between goods-producing and service-providing enterprises.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students explain the reasons businesses exist and how different types of businesses provide goods and services.

nodes.label: Why businesses exist
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify multiple reasons why businesses exist beyond profit, including employment, community service, and production of goods and services.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify two or more reasons why businesses exist, including profit and at least one non-profit reason; give a concrete local example.
nodes.typical_width: Explain why businesses exist across a range of purposes — profit, employment, providing goods and services, meeting community needs; distinguish between goods-producing and service-providing businesses using local examples including shopping centres, markets, online platforms and independent stores.
wider: Investigate a First Nations-owned business and examine its founding purposes, exploring how community, cultural and economic motivations intersect
Compare why a for-profit corporation, a not-for-profit organisation, and a cooperative exist, analysing how their purposes shape what they provide and how
Examine how remote community stores differ from urban retailers in purpose, supply constraints and community role
nodes.hinge_reason: Understanding that businesses exist for multiple reasons — not profit alone — is foundational for correctly analysing different business types in the next node. Students who reduce all business existence to profit-seeking will misclassify cooperatives, not-for-profits and First Nations enterprises, blocking meaningful engagement with business diversity.

response_modes.reason: Local community examples — including First Nations businesses, cooperatives and community stores — resolve the profit-only misconception more effectively than abstract definitions, because they make visible the genuine diversity of business purposes.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The range of business purposes across cultural, geographic and structural contexts is genuinely rich at Year 7: First Nations enterprises, remote community stores, cooperatives, and social enterprises all offer distinct and pedagogically significant cases that broaden students' understanding of what businesses are for.
success_criteria: Lists at least two distinct reasons businesses exist, beyond profit
Identifies one goods-providing and one service-providing business with an explanation of what each provides

nodes.label: Types of business structures
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify the features of different business types — sole proprietorship, partnership, cooperative, corporation, franchise, not-for-profit — and explain how structure relates to how goods and services are provided.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify at least three business types with a key distinguishing feature for each; give a real-world example of each type identified.
nodes.typical_width: Identify and describe the key features of sole proprietorship, partnership, cooperative, corporation, franchise and not-for-profit organisation; explain how each structure shapes how goods and services are provided, owned and operated; use local and national examples for each type.
wider: Analyse a cooperative — such as a First Nations community-run corporation — comparing its ownership and decision-making structure with a corporation or franchise
Investigate how franchises operate as a model: explore the relationship between franchisor and franchisee and how this shapes what the business can and cannot do
Examine how digital platforms (e.g. online marketplaces) represent newer business distribution models that sit alongside or inside traditional structures

response_modes.reason: Students need concrete exemplars for each structure type before they can apply the categories reliably. Build a running class reference of real local businesses mapped to their structure type, adding examples progressively as new structures are introduced.

success_criteria: Names and describes at least three different business types with a distinguishing feature for each
Matches a real example to each business type identified

nodes.label: Business types, goods, services and integration
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain how different types of businesses provide goods and services, connecting business structure and purpose to what is produced, how it reaches consumers, and why this matters.
nodes.minimum_width: Explain how one business type provides goods or services, connecting its structure to what it produces and how it reaches consumers.
nodes.typical_width: Explain how a range of business types provide goods and services across different distribution channels (shopping centres, markets, online, independent stores, remote community stores); analyse how business structure and purpose shape what is provided and to whom.
wider: Compare how a First Nations-owned business and a major corporation provide similar goods or services — examining differences in supply chain, ownership, community benefit and cultural purpose
Evaluate how the shift to online business has changed the types of goods and services available and which business structures benefit most from digital distribution
Investigate a social enterprise: how does its structure enable it to pursue a community mission while still operating commercially?

response_modes.reason: This node coordinates the two prior building blocks — purposes and structures — into a complete explanation of how business type shapes what is provided and how. Students should be able to reason from structure to provision, not just label the type.

success_criteria: Explains how at least two different business types provide goods or services differently, connecting structure to provision
Uses business terms (sole proprietor, corporation, cooperative, goods, services, franchise, not-for-profit) accurately in explanation
